paper_metadata.title: Association Between Early Cognitive Impairment and Midterm Functional Outcomes Among Chinese Acute Ischemic Stroke Patients: A Longitudinal Study

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study provides a clear description of the target population, recruitment period, and setting. Inclusion/exclusion criteria are explicit. While the participation rate (194/205 eligible) is high (94.6%), the sample is slightly skewed toward mild stroke (low NIHSS), which the authors acknowledge.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: We recruited patients with AIS from three major stroke centers between July and December 2016 in Shanghai, China.
items.reasoning: The source population is clearly defined as AIS patients in tertiary stroke centers in a specific geographic region.

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: The total number of patients with a final diagnosis of AIS admitted in the respective stroke centers during the enrollment period was 305. Of the 305 patients, 205 were eligible patients, and 194 patients provided informed consent.
items.reasoning: The study provides a clear flow of recruitment from the total admitted population to the final sample.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: between July and December 2016
items.reasoning: The specific months and year are provided.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: three stroke centers of tertiary hospitals in Shanghai, China.
items.reasoning: The setting (tertiary hospitals) and location (Shanghai) are specified.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: Inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) diagnosed with AIS by a neurologist or a neurosurgeon on the basis of a focal neurologic deficit and a corresponding infarct on brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)...
items.reasoning: Detailed clinical and diagnostic criteria are provided for both inclusion and exclusion.

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: 205 were eligible patients, and 194 patients provided informed consent to participate in the study.
items.reasoning: The participation rate is approximately 94.6%, which is well above the 80% threshold for low risk.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Table 2 presents the baseline sociodemographic and clinical characteristics of the patients.
items.reasoning: Comprehensive baseline data including age, sex, NIHSS, and comorbidities are reported.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The follow-up rate is excellent (94.3%). However, there is evidence of 'informative censoring' as the authors admit that those lost to follow-up had significantly lower MoCA scores (poorer cognition), which could bias the association toward the null.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: There were 194 patients at baseline and 183 patients at 6 months after onset.
items.reasoning: The attrition rate is very low (5.7%).

items.label: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out
items.prompt: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out of the study are described.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The text mentions they were unable to reach them but does not describe specific protocols or attempts to re-engage dropouts.

items.label: Reasons and potential impact of subjects lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Reasons for loss to follow-up are provided.
items.evidence_snippet: owing to inaccurate phone number or refusal to receive phone interview.
items.reasoning: Specific reasons for attrition are listed.

items.label: Outcome and prognostic factor information on those lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Participants lost to follow-up are adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: There were no statistically significant differences on age, gender, education, marital status, NIHSS, mRS, and BI between the patients who were lost to follow-up (N = 11) and those who completed the study (N = 183).
items.reasoning: The authors explicitly compared the characteristics of dropouts vs. completers.

items.prompt: There are no important differences between key characteristics (LIST) and outcomes in participants who completed the study and those who did not.
items.evidence_snippet: However, the MoCA of the patients who were lost to follow-up was significantly lower than that of those who completed the study (p < 0.05).
items.reasoning: A significant difference in the primary prognostic factor (MoCA) was found, indicating potential attrition bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The prognostic factor (Cognitive Impairment) was measured using a validated tool (MoCA-CS) by trained neurologists within a strict timeframe (7 days). The use of a validated Chinese version and clear cutoff points limits measurement bias.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: Cognitive function was assessed using Montreal Cognitive Assessment, Changsha version (MoCA-CS), within 7 days after stroke onset.
items.reasoning: The tool and timing are clearly specified.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: The MoCA-CS was tested in a sample of Chinese ischemic cerebrovascular disease patients, and the results showed that it was a reliable and valid measure
items.reasoning: The authors cite validation studies for the specific version used.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: The optimal cutoff points of MoCA-CS for detecting cognitive impairment were 26/27
items.reasoning: The cutoff used was based on prior validation literature, not derived from the current study's data.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: The neurologists administered the MoCA-CS within 7 days after the onset of stroke.
items.reasoning: Standardized administration by neurologists within a fixed window for all patients.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: 185 patients had more than two time points of data, and these patients were included into the final analysis.
items.reasoning: The analysis included the vast majority of the recruited sample with PF data.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The study does not explicitly mention how missing PF data (if any) was handled, though mixed models handle missing outcome data well.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: Outcomes (mRS and BI) are standard, validated tools in stroke research. Measurements were taken at consistent intervals. While follow-up was via telephone (subjective), these scales are validated for telephone use.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: Patients' functional outcomes were measured by modified Rankin Scale (mRS) and Barthel Index (BI) at each time point... at 1, 3, and 6 months after onset.
items.reasoning: Outcomes and follow-up schedule are clearly defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: The modified Rankin Scale (mRS) was widely used as a reliable functional abilities scale in clinical trials for stroke patients
items.reasoning: The study uses internationally recognized, validated instruments.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: administered the mRS and BI in person during the baseline and then administered them via telephone at 1, 3, and 6 months
items.reasoning: The protocol for data collection was uniform across the cohort.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study performed multivariable adjustment using Mixed Models, accounting for critical confounders including age, stroke severity (NIHSS), premorbid disability, and even treatment types (thrombolysis), which is a strength noted by the authors.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: Covariates included patient's demographic characteristics, socioeconomic status, clinical characteristics of stroke, vascular risk factors, receiving rehabilitation... and recurrence.
items.reasoning: A comprehensive list of potential confounders was collected.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: Table 1 | The list of covariates.
items.reasoning: Table 1 and the methods section provide clear coding and definitions for all covariates.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: The diagnoses of dementia and other mental disorders were obtained through a retrospective chart review.
items.reasoning: Clinical data were obtained from medical records, and standardized scales (NIHSS) were used.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: All other covariates were measured at baseline.
items.reasoning: Baseline confounders were collected uniformly during the acute hospitalization.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The text does not specify how missing covariate data was handled.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The study did not use matching or stratification in the design phase; it relied on statistical adjustment.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: Generalized linear mixed models and general linear mixed models were applied... after controlling for other covariates
items.reasoning: The authors used sophisticated longitudinal models to adjust for a wide array of confounders.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The statistical approach (Mixed Models) is appropriate for longitudinal data with multiple time points. Results are reported with Odds Ratios and Beta coefficients with 95% CIs. There is no evidence of selective reporting.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: The procedure of PROC GLIMMIX and PROC MIXED in SAS Version 9.4... was used
items.reasoning: The software and specific procedures are named, and the modeling steps are described.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: Then only the statistically significant independent variables (p < 0.05) were entered into the multivariate generalized linear mixed models
items.reasoning: The authors used a standard step-wise approach based on univariate significance.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: Generalized linear mixed models and general linear mixed models were applied.
items.reasoning: Mixed models are the gold standard for analyzing trajectories in longitudinal data with missingness.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: Table 3 presents the results... Table 4 presents the results
items.reasoning: The authors report on all pre-specified outcomes (mRS and BI) and provide full model results.
